title: Abuse: what to do
summary: If someone hits you, insults you, locks you in or keeps food from you, it is not your fault. Here is how to stay safe and get help.

title: Arriving home at Bole airport
summary: What usually happens when returnees land in Addis Ababa, and what help you can ask for with food, shelter, health, counselling and getting home.

title: Claiming unpaid wages after you are home
summary: Getting your unpaid pay from home is hard, but you can still try. Keep your evidence and ask the embassy, your agency and legal helpers.

title: Contacting your embassy
summary: The Ethiopian embassy or consulate is there to help Ethiopians abroad. Here is what it can and cannot do, what to say, and what to have ready.

title: Contraception and sexual health before you go
summary: Your body, your choice. Learn about contraception, protection from infections, and the laws on pregnancy in some destination countries, so you can decide what is right for you.

title: If you are detained or deported
summary: Being held in a deportation centre is frightening, but you still have rights. You can ask for your embassy, for medical care and for help to travel home.

title: Copy your important documents
summary: Take photos of your passport, visa, contract and other papers before you leave. Keep copies in safe places, and keep important numbers on paper too.

title: Family and community after you return
summary: Coming home can bring money pressure, gossip and shame. What happened is not your fault, and you can choose what to share.

title: If I leave my employer's house, will I be in trouble with the law?
summary: It can be risky.

title: The agency is asking me for a lot of money. Is that allowed?
summary: Be careful.

title: How do I contact the Ethiopian embassy, and what can they do?
summary: The embassy and consulate numbers for your country are in Help numbers in DadaLink.

title: Can I change to a different employer?
summary: Sometimes, yes, but the rules are very different in each country and often need the labour ministry, the employer or the agency to agree.

title: How can I avoid getting pregnant while I work abroad?
summary: This is your choice and your body.

title: My job or salary is different from what my contract says. What can I do?
summary: Your signed contract is what counts.

title: I was arrested or I am in a deportation centre. What are my rights?
summary: You can ask to contact the Ethiopian embassy or consulate.

title: Which documents should I copy before I leave?
summary: Take clear photos of your passport, visa, signed contract, Ethiopian ID, the agency's name and licence, and your employer's name, address and phone.

title: My employer hits me or threatens me. What can I do?
summary: No one has the right to hurt you.

title: A broker says he can send me abroad quickly without an agency. Is it safe?
summary: This is risky.

title: I am locked in the house and not given enough food. What can I do?
summary: Being locked in or kept hungry is abuse, and it can be a sign of forced labour or trafficking.

title: I feel very lonely and sad all the time. Is something wrong with me?
summary: Nothing is wrong with you.

title: I never get a day off. Is that allowed?
summary: You deserve rest.

title: My employer took my passport. What can I do?
summary: This happens to many women.

title: I think I am pregnant. I am scared. What should I do?
summary: It is normal to feel scared.

title: I just came back and I feel lost. Where can I get support?
summary: Coming home can be hard, even when you are glad to be back.

title: Someone forced me into sex. What can I do?
summary: I am so sorry this happened.

title: I am sick and my employer will not take me to a doctor. What should I do?
summary: Your health matters.

title: I do not want to live anymore.
summary: I am really glad you told me.

title: I work from early morning to late at night and I am always tired. What can I do?
summary: Very long hours with no sleep are harmful, and it is right to ask for rest.

title: My employer has not paid my salary. What should I do?
summary: You have a right to be paid what your contract says.

title: I came home but my employer still owes me money. Can I still get it?
summary: It is harder after you return, but sometimes possible.

title: I want to go home before my contract ends. How?
summary: You can ask for help to go home.

title: A health check after you come home
summary: A check-up after you return helps you find and treat problems early, including infections that have no signs. You deserve care with respect.

title: Getting ready for your health
summary: You will need a medical check before you go. Plan for your medicines, because some medicines are controlled in Gulf countries.

title: Leaving a bad employer safely
summary: If your job is unsafe or unfair, there are legal ways to leave. Running away without a plan can cause serious problems. Here is how to protect yourself.

title: Laws that may be different abroad
summary: Some things that are normal at home can be against the law in your new country. Knowing the main rules helps you stay safe.

title: Licensed agencies and illegal brokers
summary: Go abroad only through an agency licensed by the Ministry of Labour and Skills. Illegal brokers and smuggling routes put your life and your rights in danger.

title: Feeling lonely, sad or stressed
summary: Missing home, feeling sad or worried is normal. Here are small things that can help, signs you need more help, and what to do if you feel you cannot go on.

title: Taking care of your mind after you return
summary: Stress, sadness, anger, bad dreams and shame are common after hard experiences. You are not alone, and help is available.

title: Money and work after you return
summary: Protect your savings, look for skills and business support, and if you want to go abroad again, use only a licensed agency.

title: Money, fees and debt
summary: Know which costs you may have to pay and which you should not pay. Avoid debt to brokers, send money home safely, and keep a record of your wages.

title: My employer took my passport
summary: Your passport belongs to you. Here is what the law says in some countries, and safe steps you can take if your employer keeps it.

title: I think I am pregnant
summary: Finding out you are pregnant far from home can be frightening. You are not alone. Here is how to look after your health and get confidential help.

title: Getting ready to go home
summary: Before you leave, try to collect your pay, keep copies of your papers and know who pays for your ticket. Your embassy can help with travel documents.

title: Rest, sleep and my day off
summary: You need rest to stay healthy. Many countries give domestic workers daily rest and a weekly day off. Keep a log and know where to complain.

title: Your rights as a domestic worker in the United Arab Emirates
summary: A UAE law protects domestic workers. You have the right to a written contract, pay on time, rest every day and every week, and to keep your own passport.

title: Your rights before you go and when you come home (Ethiopia)
summary: Ethiopia's Overseas Employment Proclamation No. 1389/2025 protects you before you leave, while you work abroad, and when you come home. Agencies may not take money from you for finding you a job, and you can complain to the Ministry of Labour and Skills.

title: Your rights as a domestic worker in Jordan
summary: In Jordan, a special regulation under the Labour Law gives domestic workers rights to pay, rest, leave and health care. Keeping your passport from you is a crime, and there are places to complain and get help.

title: Your rights as a domestic worker in Kuwait
summary: Kuwait's Domestic Workers Law (Law No. 68 of 2015) protects you. You have the right to a contract, monthly pay with no deductions, a weekly day off, 30 days of paid leave, and to keep your own passport.

title: Your rights as a domestic worker in Lebanon
summary: In Lebanon, domestic workers are not covered by the Labour Law. Your rights come mainly from the standard contract you sign, and there are people who can help if those rights are broken.

title: Your rights as a domestic worker in Qatar
summary: Qatar's Domestic Workers Law (Law No. 15 of 2017) and the minimum wage law protect you. You have the right to a contract, at least QAR 1,000 a month, a weekly day off, and to change jobs or go home.

title: Your rights as a domestic worker in Saudi Arabia
summary: Saudi Arabia has a special regulation for domestic workers. It gives you a contract, monthly pay, a weekly day off, limits on working hours, and says your employer must not keep your passport.

title: Sexual violence: what to do
summary: If someone touched you or forced you into a sexual act, it is not your fault. Get safe, get medical care quickly, and choose what happens next.

title: I am sick or injured
summary: Your health comes first. In many countries your employer must give you medical care. Here is what to do and how to keep records.

title: Your trusted person and safety plan
summary: Choose one person at home who will always look out for you. Agree a plan together before you leave, so they know when and how to get help.

title: My employer is not paying my salary
summary: You have the right to be paid for your work. Keep a record of every payment and know where to complain.

title: Your work contract
summary: Before you leave, get a written contract in a language you understand. Check every detail, and keep a copy and a photo.
